title: How Passports Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explain how passports work: the etymology debate over the word "passport," early history (Nehemiah's safe-conduct, King John and freedom of movement, the UN Universal Declaration of Human Rights), how passport requirements developed in Europe and the US, passport size history, and the practical process of getting a US passport (forms DS-11, DS-82 renewal, fees, timelines, in-person requirements, passport cards, the Western Hemisphere Travel Initiative backlog in 2007, same-day expedited options). They also cover photo requirements, lacking a birth certificate (letter of no record, DS-10 and DS-71 affidavits), the passport as government property, proposed passport revocation laws, and camouflage passports. The episode closes with a listener mail from David about male privilege and the complexities of gender.

segments.title: Opening banter and episode setup
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck introduce the passport episode as informational and note it is aimed at people who need to get a US passport.

segments.title: Origin of the word passport and early history
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the competing etymologies of 'passport' (British 'pass through a port' versus French 'porte' meaning gate), then trace early precedents such as Nehemiah's request for safe passage in the Bible and King John's role in freedom of movement.

segments.title: Passports in Europe and the United States
segments.summary: Covers the UN Universal Declaration of Human Rights on freedom of movement, British passport records and photos and old physical descriptions, Europe abandoning passports in the 1860s, US passport requirements beginning around the Civil War, universal adoption during World War One, and the oversized early US passport shrinking to a three by five format.

segments.title: How to apply for a US passport
segments.summary: Explains application options including post offices, passport agencies in all fifty states, and printing form DS-11 at home. First-time applicants must apply in person with proof of identity and sign in front of an acceptance agent. Costs are discussed as one hundred five dollars for adults and children for first passports, with renewals cheaper by mail. Validity is ten years for adults and five for those under sixteen.

segments.title: Processing times, stamps, and the Western Hemisphere Travel Initiative
segments.summary: Discusses the State Department's estimate of four to six weeks for processing and advice to apply months ahead. Covers passport stamps varying by country. Describes the 2007 Western Hemisphere Travel Initiative, which required passports for air travel and introduced the cheaper passport card for land and sea travel, and the resulting backlog of about fifteen weeks, with a warning about the ten-year renewal wave.

segments.title: When in-person application is required and proving identity
segments.summary: Lists situations requiring an in-person visit: first passports, lost or stolen passports, expired passports issued more than fifteen years ago, passports issued under age sixteen, and name changes without legal documentation. Covers proof of birth via a letter of no record and supporting documents such as census records, baptismal certificates, and family Bible records, plus forms DS-10 and DS-71 for blood relatives or acquaintances vouching for identity.

segments.title: Emergency and same-day passports
segments.summary: Describes getting a passport quickly in life-and-death situations, rush appointments at regional passport offices with a sixty dollar rush fee, and private expediting agencies charging roughly one hundred eighty to three hundred dollars for same-day or eight-hour service.

segments.title: Passport photo requirements
segments.summary: Details the specifications: two by two inch color photo, front-facing, head size between one and one-third and one and three-eighths inches, neutral expression with a slight smile allowed, no hats or sunglasses unless worn daily, and white or off-white background. Suggests professional photo services such as drugstores.

segments.title: Passport ownership, E-passports, and revocation debates; camouflage passports
segments.summary: Notes the passport is property of the US government and must be surrendered on request. Describes the RFID chip in e-passports, which originated in Malaysia, and anti-forgery features that Nicaragua pioneered. Discusses proposed laws to revoke passports for unpaid taxes, child support, or terrorist association, and critics' concerns about assassination. Mentions camouflage passports created by Donna Walker and fraud risks, and advice to keep copies of passports.

segments.title: Listener mail from David on male privilege
segments.summary: David writes about being a gay, introverted man who experienced disadvantages related to his gender, and says the hosts' jokes about men were a mistake. Josh and Chuck agree it is one of the best listener mails and invite listeners to share feedback.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts sign off and direct listeners to social media, email, and the website for more information.
